I'm 61 years old, and I've been farming these flat fields in Quzhou since I was a boy. I only finished primary school, but I know this land and this climate better than any book. Around here, the only sensible thing is to grow winter wheat followed by summer maize on the same plot — my father did it, my neighbors do it, and the grain buyers in town expect it. I have about 8 mu of good irrigated land, and I won't gamble on anything fancy at my age.

For the wheat I sowed last October, I use the improved variety from the county seed station — it's reliable and resists the rust we sometimes get. After the maize harvest in autumn, I always run the rotary tiller to break up the stalks before sowing wheat. For fertilizer, I put down compound fertilizer at planting, then topdress with urea when the wheat greens up and at jointing. I'd rather be safe than sorry when my family depends on the harvest. The wheat needs three good irrigations: before winter sets in, at jointing in spring, and at heading. I spray for weeds once after sowing and for insects twice in spring if I see aphids.

Right after cutting the wheat in early June, I plant summer maize straight into the stubble without tilling — there's no time to waste, and the summer season is short. I always buy hybrid seed from the shop; the hybrids yield much better than anything else. I apply compound fertilizer at sowing, and if the plants look yellow, a little extra urea. Summer maize usually only needs two irrigations because the rains come, but I watch the sky. I spray once for weeds and once for corn borer.

I expect around 500 kg per mu for the wheat and about 550 kg per mu for the maize if the weather is normal. That's been my average most years.
